Torrential downpours expected to spread north across England and Wales | UK weather

After sweltering in temperatures that touched on 32C (89.6F), the UK is now braced for torrential downpours and storms that could cause flash-flooding across large parts of the country.

The Environment Agency warned that up to 30mm (1.2in) of rain could fall in an hour in some areas.

The agency says that almost every county in England and Wales is at medium risk of flooding today, and has issued 59 flood alerts, warning people to be prepared.

The majority of these are in the Midlands, the south-east and the south-west

In a separate amber warning of rain for England, eastern and central Wales, the Met Office warns that heavy, thundery showers that developed overnight will move northwards during the day.

Large amounts of energy in the atmosphere will lead to torrential downpours, frequent lightning, large hail and strong gusts of wind.

The Met Office said: "Not everywhere within the warning area will see thunderstorms, and indeed some spells of warm sunshine are expected at times, but where thunderstorms do form, some torrential downpours are likely with frequent lightning, large hail and locally strong gusts.

"Significant flooding is possible where these do occur from surface water as well as from small, fast-responding watercourses. The public should be prepared for the risk of disruption from any of these elements."

There is still, however, a yellow warning of a heatwave for the UK today, advising people to be "alert and ready". The Met Office said there was a 60% chance of a heatwave continuing until tomorrow morning, with high levels of humidity.

John Curtin, director of incident management at the Environment Agency, said: "Intense heavy rainfall this weekend brings a surface water flood risk for England throughout the weekend. Flooding can happen very quickly and the public are urged to keep checking local weather forecasts and the Environment Agency website for information on a regular basis.

"We will continue to monitor the situation closely and support local authorities, who will respond to any reports of surface water flooding. We will also continue to monitor river levels closely and issue warnings where flooding is likely."

Storms hit large parts of the south-east of England early on Friday morning, with a reported 3,000 lightning strikes.

Gemma Plumb, a forecaster with MeteoGroup, said: "Today we have got some heavy and severe thunderstorms continuing to spread north across the UK. Most of the UK is going to see some heavy showers or long spells of rain during the day and severe thunderstorms.

"These could give hail, gusty winds and very frequent lightning strikes.

"It will not be as hot as yesterday, but it will still be very warm and humid. East Anglia could still see temperatures as high as 27C (80.6F) to 29C (84.2F), Kent will see 27C (80.6F) or 28C (82.4F), rather than the 32C (89.6F) it had yesterday."

Fire crews have been called to a number of incidents caused by lightning.

The first floor and roof of a house in Sittingbourne, Kent, was set alight by a strike, while a bungalow's roof was hit in Whitstable, Kent fire and eescue said.

Houses were struck in the market village of Lenham, near Maidstone, while lightning also started several small fires in Willesborough, near Ashford.

A spokeswoman for Heathrow airport said airlines were cancelling 20% of flights for a two-hour period today due to the thundery weather.

She said: "There is severe weather forecast at Heathrow with a 70% risk of thunderstorms, lightning strikes and hail storms. During thunderstorms the number of aircraft that can take off and land each hour is reduced.

"We have therefore requested that airlines reduce their flight schedule by 20% between 4pm and 6pm. Passengers due to travel on 19 July are urged to check the status of their flight with their airline before travelling to the airport."

Patients on a hospital ward had to be moved when heavy rain brought down part of a ceiling.

Twenty-seven patients on the cardiology ward at the Royal United hospital in Bath, Somerset, were transferred after the incident at around 2am.

Three ceiling panels came down in the hospital's catheter lab and cardiology ward after the roof sprang a leak.

The patients, who were all unharmed, were taken to other parts of the hospital.

A hospital spokesman said: "At about 2am, in one of the severe heavy storms we had last night across the south-west, there was a leak sprung in the roof of the hospital.

"Water got into the roof, causing three of the ceiling panels to come down due to the weight of the water.

"We had to transfer 27 patients from the cardiology ward to other parts of the hospital. They were not injured but they were inconvenienced and we apologise for that."

The leak has now been plugged and it is hoped that the patients will soon be able to return to the ward, the spokesman added.

A spokeswoman for South Western ambulance service said an officer attended the hospital at 2.50am to liaise with medics but no further assistance was required.

Check out these ‘epic’ images from that surprise lightning storm – Orange County Register

Lightning fills the sky over North Tustin as a storm moved through parts of Orange County late Thursday night, September 9, 2021. (Photo by Mark Rightmire, Orange County Register/SCNG)

1 of 16

Lightning fills the sky over North Tustin as a storm moved through parts of Orange County late Thursday night, September 9, 2021. (Photo by Mark Rightmire, Orange County Register/SCNG)

Expand

A surprise lightning and thunderstorm raced into Orange County late Thursday, as spectators and photographers marveled at the show in the sky.

It also brought a shot of much-needed rain to parts of the region.

National Weather Service meteorologist Adam Roser said a monsoon pattern system from moist air coming up from Mexico caused the storm in San Diego, which then came rolling into San Clemente.

“The atmosphere was unstable enough to support thunderstorm activity in areas of the coast,” he said. “Some storms started to bubble up, in San Diego and Orange County and over the ocean as well.”

The lightning in San Diego as it made its way up the coast could be seen from San Clemente by about 8 p.m., with flashes in the distance happening every 30 seconds to a minute. Then after 9 p.m., the storm hit Orange County.

The NWS San Diego office, which also covers Orange County, put out a tally on how many lightning strikes hit from cloud to ground, reporting 81 strikes along the San Diego coast and ocean, and 20 the mountains. It did not have Orange County numbers. Riverside mountains had 93 strikes while the Inland Empire had 153. San Bernardino Mountains experienced 30.

Lightning also struck the mountains of the Angeles National Forest.

“There’s always a chance some of the storms might go over the coast and valleys, but it’s usually quite minimal. There’s always a slight chance – most of the time it stays in mountains and deserts,” he said. “Anytime it does, it’s a fun time and a good sign, a little bit of rain in some areas.”

Orange County didn’t get much rain, but every drop helps as drought conditions persist. The Orange County reservoir recorded a quarter of an inch, while Laguna Hills got 0.1 inches.

“Not enough to put a dent in the drought, but anything can help this dry time of year,” Roser said. “Hopefully we see a little more as we get into the cooler months.”

The bright shots from the sky had photographers scrambling to capture images of the rare event.

Matt Larmand, of Capistrano Beach, set up his camera on the north end of San Clemente to get images of bolts just beyond the iconic pier.

“It was so epic, best lightning show I’ve ever seen,” he said in an online message. “There were a few bolts that were pretty close to us and a few right overhead. Was a little nervous for a few minutes!”

Royce Hutain traveled from Huntington Beach to get a few shots, including one of lightning just over a tree in San Clemente. When the hair on his legs started standing up, he said he knew it was time to leave.

Torrance photographer Patrick Coyne scored an unbelievable video with bioluminescence creating a neon flash in the waves at the same time lightning flashed to light up the sky off Laguna Beach’s coastline.

Roser said the mountain regions and deserts may still get some of the monsoonal moisture today, but it’s not expected again on the coast.

The weather should start to stabilize Friday and through the weekend. It will remain warm with 90s inland and a little cooler on the coast, with a high-pressure system lingering before cooling early next week, Roser said.

Big surf is also on the way, with a swell building Saturday and into Sunday bringing 3-foot to 5-foot surf, with a second swell early next week that could deliver waves in the 6-foot to 8-foot range, Roser said.

Adoption should be the last port of call – even in the storm of local authority funding | Social Care Network

The language judges use is usually considered and restrained, but there are times when they make their displeasure clear. Last year, addressing a mother’s appeal against a court’s refusal to let her oppose the adoption of her children, president of the high court’s family division Sir James Munby stated: “We have real concerns, shared by other judges, about the recurrent inadequacy of the analysis and reasoning put forward in support of the case for adoption, both in the materials put before the court by local authorities and guardians and also in too many judgments. This is nothing new. But it is time to call a halt.”

The mother in Re B-S – the name of the case – did in fact lose her appeal, and therefore lost her children too: her barrister feels her grounds for appeal were not fully addressed by the court. Nevertheless, reading through the judgment it is evident that Munby felt he had to restate the stringent requirements made of social workers and lower courts. This is based on legislation that sets out how the state must evaluate, support and ensure the welfare of a child thought to be at serious risk of harm.


Adoption should be the last option

Re B-S is now transforming the way that local authorities plan for the futures of children they seek to remove from their family home. While this is welcomed in principle by adoption professionals, there is also a significant tension between the aims of government – to get more children adopted faster and more adopters approved quicker – and legislation that high court judges are underlining. This essentially means that adoption cannot become the default option for financially stretched local authorities, and is only suitable where nothing else will do.

“This opens up options of other measures that don’t terminate the legal links between a parent and a child, such as care orders or guardianship,” says John Simmonds, policy director at the British Association for Adoption and Fostering (BAAF). “It has also raised the issue that local authorities cannot use adoption to avoid providing appropriate supportive services to families so they can better look after their children themselves.

“The message from the president (of the family division) and the supreme court is that there may be many families out there that we don’t like but that is not the same as saying that we should remove their children and put them with better families.”

Money is stretched painfully tight at the moment, but not wanting to cough up for expensive or long-term family interventions that could enable a parent, or perhaps a relative, to care for the child, was dealt with severely in the judgment. “The local authority cannot press for a more drastic form or order, least of all press for adoption, because it is unable or unwilling to support a less interventionist form of order,” it said. “Judges must be alert to the point and must be rigorous in exploring and probing local authority thinking in cases where there is any reason to suspect that resource issues may be affecting the local authority’s thinking.”


A need for joined-up thinking

This gives rise to a hollow laugh from barrister Maureen Obi of Family Matters Chambers, who represented the mother in Re B-S.

“I’ve represented numerous teenage parents for instance, and there are no resources there to help teenage mums,” she says. “They have to fit into adult services and very often they are still children themselves, with entirely different needs. The outcome is they have their babies taken away and adopted. The reality then is that these parents are just left.”

There are, Obi points out, specialist organisations that can offer effective help to struggling parents in a range of situations, but in many cases the child’s welfare ends up being separated from the parents’ issues and so the situation is not holistically addressed. “The difficulty is that there is no co-ordinated approach to getting services to parents,” she argues. “Local authority [adult’s and children’s] services don’t join up their thinking and the courts don’t join up their thinking.”

Re B-S makes it clear that councils cannot argue that a particular intervention is too expensive. But is there enough funding available for support that would give people the best chance of parenting their children well?

At Stockport council, director of children’s services and immediate past president of the Association of Directors of Children’s Services Andrew Webb draws a deep breath. “The answer to that is a very qualified yes” he says. But there are clearly caveats.

Webb points out that councils have seen a 30% cut in their preventive services grant, and have two more years of cuts to absorb. He also notes that around a third of all care proceedings relate to families where children have already been taken away. Women frequently have more babies to replace the children they have lost, and Webb acknowledges that addressing this particular spiral of despair is “an area we really do need to work on, where we do not have the resources in place.”


Permanency plans must be completed in six months

The comments made in Re B-S about poor evidence gathering by social workers and badly argued cases for placement and adoption orders being nodded through lower courts have created huge difficulties for child protection teams. They are now told they have to get children’s permanency plans signed off within 26 weeks. There is no doubt that social workers have to get better at this part of the job, says Mark Owers, chief executive of the Consortium for Voluntary Adoption Agencies. “The quality of social worker decision making has been variable for decades and we have known about it and have done nothing about it,” he says. “The Care Enquiry addressed it and we did not take it on board.”

At BAAF John Simmonds agrees, but says a loss of confidence is becoming apparent in social workers and the lower courts about how to proceed in these serious child welfare cases. “It is absolutely right that it can’t be done in any way that’s not thought through or without good enough evidence,” Simmonds says. But social care professionals are working in an urgent environment. “For children to wait [for permanence] is not the right thing. We do need a confident, clear, coherent structure to make this work within the child’s time frame.”

A year on, the impact of Re B-S is plain, says Owers. “There has been a significant fall in the number of placement orders and agency decision making [for adoption] as a direct result of Re B-S and other similar cases,” he says. And at the coalface, Beth Prince, a solicitor for children in care and advisor to the Family Rights Group, testifies to an immediate about-turn in the attitude of one local authority to a family’s situation.

“The day that Re B-S came out I was representing a baby in care proceedings,” she recalls. “The parents were unable to look after it. But there was a grandmother. The guardian [appointed to represent the child’s interests] had thought she was nice, but hadn’t seriously considered her as a carer. And yet when the grandmother gave evidence the guardian was very impressed.”

At this point, Prince says, the guardian was very keen to explore what the options might be. Overnight she redrafted a new position statement asking for a reassessment of the grandmother as a carer for the baby. “I was a bit anxious about telling the local authority barrister the next day,” says Prince, “but she came up to me, thrust the Re B-S judgement into my hand and said “this changes everything.””

The local authority solicitor agreed with Prince’s new application. Nothing was guaranteed at this point, Prince points out, “but what happened was that the grandmother was reassessed, and in the end, she got the baby.”

Prince believes it’s essential for local authorities to be challenged more rigorously on their evidence and reasoning when they’re asking for placement and adoption orders. “Local authorities can be punitive in borderline cases,” she says. She has seen cases where parents have made significant improvements and, despite this being acknowledged within social services’ own documentation, councils still “persist on the route towards a care order or adoption order.”

It then takes the parents’ or child’s legal representative to point out the discrepancy between the improvements that social workers have documented, and the continued demand for the removal of a child. Even when a lawyer is successful and a judge throws out an application, for a parent who is likely to be vulnerable, the experience is traumatic.


Intervention before care proceedings

In Stockport, Webb says that he now expects to see significant changes in how his social work teams approach the task of protecting children.

“Once you make a decision to initiate care proceedings, it’s entirely reasonable to expect those to be resolved within six months, so the key is then what you do beforehand,” he says.

He wants far more work to be done with vulnerable families on the edge of care in advance of applying to remove a child from their home “so lots of intervention and support to families before care proceedings are initiated,” he explains.

As a result of pulling all such child protection assessments and support into the pre-court phase, he hopes families will cope better and far fewer children will remain at risk. This will reduce the number of applications to a court, and mean “that when a court asks if you have the evidence to say “no, there’s no other alternative [than adoption]”, you can say ‘yes, and here it all is.’”
